source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use clean technique for fistula cannulation because bloodstream-infection prevention measures are needed only when a dialysis catheter is being accessed.","B":"Skip access-site preparation when the fistula skin appears intact, because visible cleanliness is sufficient after the nurse has completed hand hygiene.","C":"Reuse a vascular-access needle for the same client if it remains visibly clean, because repeated cannulation does not require a new sterile device each time.","D":"Use aseptic technique whenever the vascular access is cannulated and follow the facility's standardized access-care practices each time the fistula is used."}}
source_row.rationale: Hand hygiene is necessary, but CDC dialysis-safety guidance also emphasizes aseptic vascular-access care and staff competency. Option D correctly adds aseptic technique and standardized access practices to hand hygiene. Option A incorrectly limits aseptic precautions to dialysis catheters. Option B skips access-site preparation based on appearance alone. Option C proposes reuse of a vascular-access needle, which is inconsistent with sterile single-use access practice.
source_row.source_detail: CDC Dialysis Safety — Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention: staff training and competency in vascular-access care and aseptic technique; observe adherence to aseptic technique during vascular-access care/cannulation. Current CDC dialysis-safety clinical guidance at cited URL; rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: asepsis, equipment/environmental safety, incident/event prevention and infection-control activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene before cannulating a client's arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis. Which additional infection-prevention principle is essential?
